title: Motor Stopped Unexpectedly
description: Diagnose why the motor stopped while it should be running

n1.text: Alright, let's start at the contactor. Go check K1 in the starter panel — is the contactor pulled in? You should hear it click when someone hits the start button.
n1.hint: Look for the main motor contactor. When energized, the armature should be pulled in tight with no buzzing.

options.label: Yes, it's energized
options.transition: Good, it's energized. Power is getting through to the contactor at least.

options.label: No, it's not pulling in
options.transition: OK so the contactor isn't pulling in. Let's figure out why.

n2.text: Contactor's in but motor isn't running. Check all 3 phases at the motor terminals with your meter. Getting voltage on all three?
n2.hint: Measure L1-L2, L2-L3, L1-L3 at the motor terminal box. All three should be within 2% of each other.

options.label: Yes, all three phases present
options.transition: Voltage at the motor but it won't spin — that's a motor problem.

options.label: Missing one or more phases
options.transition: Lost a phase somewhere between the contactor and the motor.

options.label: No voltage at all
options.transition: Contactor's in but no voltage at the motor — there's a break in the wiring.

n3.text: Check the overload relay next — is the red trip flag showing?
n3.hint: The thermal overload relay (OLR) is usually mounted directly below the contactor. Look for a red trip indicator or a popped reset button.

options.label: Yes, it's tripped
options.transition: The overload tripped. That means the motor was drawing too much current before it stopped.

options.label: No, looks normal
options.transition: Good, that rules out the overload. Now let's check the control circuit.

n4.text: Grab your meter and measure across the contactor coil terminals A1 and A2. Getting any voltage?
n4.hint: The coil voltage should match the control circuit — typically 24VDC or 120VAC depending on the design.

options.label: Yes, voltage is there
options.transition: Voltage at the coil but it won't pull in — that's your answer.

options.label: No voltage
options.transition: No coil voltage. Something upstream in the control circuit is open.

n5.text: Let's trace the control circuit. Check these in order: Is the start/stop station wired correctly? Any auxiliary contacts in series that might be open? Any safety interlocks (door switches, light curtains)?
n5.hint: The control circuit is a series loop — any one open contact breaks it. Check the simplest things first: stop button not latched, door switch open.

options.label: Found an open interlock/switch
options.transition: There it is. An open interlock is killing the control circuit.

options.label: Everything looks closed
options.transition: Control circuit looks intact but still no coil voltage. Let's check the source.

n6.text: Check the control power source. Is the control transformer or 24V power supply outputting correct voltage?
n6.hint: Measure at the secondary of the control transformer, or the output of the 24V supply. Should match the coil rating.

options.label: Yes, control power is good
options.transition: OK this is getting tricky — control power is good, circuit looks complete, but no coil voltage.

options.label: No, control power is dead
options.transition: No control power — that explains everything.

n_seized.text: Motor has voltage on all phases but won't turn. It's likely mechanically seized or has an internal winding failure.
steps: Lock out and tag out the motor disconnect
Try rotating the shaft by hand — if it won't turn, the motor is seized
Check all 3 phase-to-phase winding resistances with a megger or ohmmeter
If seized: check bearings, coupling, and driven load
If windings are bad: motor needs to be replaced or rewound

n_phase.text: Single-phasing — you've lost a phase between the contactor and motor. Running on two phases will burn up a motor fast.
steps: Lock out and tag out immediately
Check each wire from contactor output to motor terminals for continuity
Inspect contactor tips for pitting or welding — a burned contact won't pass current
Check for any fuses in the motor branch circuit
Repair the open circuit and megg the motor windings before restarting

n_wiring.text: Contactor is engaged but no voltage at the motor. There's a break somewhere in the power wiring.
steps: Lock out and tag out at the main disconnect
Check continuity from contactor load-side terminals to motor terminals
Inspect any disconnect switches or fused disconnects between contactor and motor
Look for damaged conduit or pulled wires, especially near flex connections

n_overload.text: The thermal overload tripped, which means the motor was overcurrent before it stopped. Don't just reset it — figure out why it tripped first.
steps: Wait 5 minutes for the OLR bimetal strips to cool
Check for obvious causes: jam, heavy load, binding
Verify the OLR is set to the correct FLA (check motor nameplate)
Reset the overload relay (press the blue reset button)
Restart and monitor current closely for the first few minutes
If it trips again, run the motor-overcurrent troubleshoot guide

n_contactor_bad.text: Voltage at the coil but it won't pull in — the contactor is faulty. The coil might be open or the mechanism is jammed.
steps: Lock out and tag out the motor disconnect
Measure the contactor coil resistance (should be a few hundred ohms, not open)
If coil is open: replace the contactor
If coil reads OK: check for mechanical binding in the contactor
Make sure the replacement has the same coil voltage rating
Test before putting back in service

n_interlock.text: An open safety interlock or auxiliary contact was holding the control circuit open. That's actually the system working as designed — something triggered it.
steps: Identify which interlock is open and WHY it opened
Don't bypass safety interlocks — fix the condition that triggered them
Close the guard door, clear the light curtain, or address whatever opened the interlock
Verify the control circuit is complete, then try starting again

n_control_power.text: The control power source is dead — no voltage to drive any of the control circuitry. Everything downstream (contactors, relays, PLC outputs) is unpowered.
steps: Check the control transformer primary fuse or breaker
If it's a 24V supply, check its input power and output LED
Replace fuse or reset breaker if tripped
If the transformer or supply is dead, it needs replacement
Once control power is restored, verify all interlocks clear and try restarting

n_llm.text: We've checked the obvious causes and haven't found the issue. This might need someone with a scope or more detailed prints to trace the control logic further.
steps: Review the electrical drawings for the full control circuit
Check for PLC-controlled outputs in the start circuit
Look for any timer or sequencing relays that might be holding the circuit open
If available, use PLC diagnostics to check output states
